COMMENTS: Mololo Cave (WAI-1 in the Raja Ampat Archaeological Project database) is located at the entrance to Mayalibit Bay, the large water body that almost bisects Waigeo. It is a limestone system comprised of a light outer chamber, exposed to sunlight but sheltered from rain, and a dark inner chamber that is home to several bat colonies.

COMMENTS: Description: In this site, 184 rock drawings were identified that consisted of drawings of humans (4), anthropomorphic (2), fish (20), sea cucumbers (8), jelly fish (2), sea horses (4), turtles (2), lizards (1), snakes (1), four legged animals (1), fish tail (1), hand stencils (33), spears (1), arrows (5), axes (2), geometric shapes (23), circles (5), roundular shapes (15), patterned wheels (2), lines (1), parallel lines (3), and several other unidentified objects (52). Based on the types of the drawings, the rock art in this site consisted of 20 dotted-line drawings, 26 line drawings, 41 outline drawings, and 29 solid infill drawings, and 68 negative drawings. From the technique of the drawing, there were 95 brush drawings, and there were 88 drawings that used the spraying technique, consisting of images of hand stencils, axes, decorated wheels, sea horses, fish tails and geometrical shapes. In creating the hand stencils under the spraying technique, the hands were pressed against the wall and then sprayed with coloring. However, in making the fine and beautiful patterns of the decorated wheels, the creators used a certain molding that was placed on the wall and then it was sprayed with coloring. | Keywords: papua, west papua, misool

COMMENTS: Description: The Dolphin Site is located 1o57’48.31” South Latitude and 130o27’34.27” East Longitude. In this site, there are nine patterns consisting of eight hand stencils and one fish drawing. There were two techniques applied in making the drawings, first the brush technique that was used in drawing the fish image and the second is the spray technique applied in making the hand stencils with red coloring and facing upward. The fish figures are solid infill drawings that depict dolphins positioned in between hand stencils facing upward. Meanwhile, the hand stencils are negative-type patterns and all of them are images of the right hand super-positioned (overlapping). The hand stencils were not decorated, and there were four objects only showing fingers and the palm and another four objects showing fingers up to the wrist. There were six drawings facing upward and two drawings facing the left or facing each other. The chamber in the cliff rock is ± 2 meters long measured from end to end of the drawings, while the height of the drawings measured from the sea level to the closest drawing is ± 3 meters above sea level, facing the west. The rock art in this site is in good condition. | Keywords: papua, west papua, misool

COMMENTS: At Manwen Bokor, some red pottery fragments are similar to pots made along the north coast of New Guinea. Other ceramics from the site include 'circle stamp' designs that are similar to decorations used throughout northern Maluku as well as other parts of Island Southeast Asia like Banda, Sulawesi, and even Taiwan. At Manwen Bokor, the archaeologists also uncovered glazed ceramics that were produced in China and exported to Southeast Asia, eventually arriving to Raja Ampat. On the surface of a large cliff overlooking the site, the team also recovered two yellow glass beads that may have been produced on the mainland of Southeast Asia or in India, before being traded along the Indian Ocean rim to eventually arrive on Waigeo. Beads like these would have been used for decoration, exchanges, marriage ceremonies, and even to decorate ancestor figurines.

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-31 Lentagin (known by this name in the local Kawe Ma'ya dialect) consists of a large limestone cliff face approximately 50 m high and 100 m long, facing east onto Aljui Bay. A single gallery about 10 m long is located 5-7 m above the present high-tide mark and contains red and orange pigment designs. The imagery is divided into four clusters. Cluster 1: two red and one orange hand stencils, a stencil of an unknown three-pointed object, and further faded red hand stencils below. Cluster 2: a dotted image in four columns and nine rows (finger-painted), a segmented ovoid, two hand stencils, simplified anthropomorphs (vertical lines), possible fish or marine animals (horizontal lines), and a black pigment design superimposed over a red hand stencil, possibly an abstracted anthropomorph. Cluster 3: partly obscured by water action, contains segmented circular and ovoid motifs and a dotted orange pigment quadrangle subdivided into three parts. Cluster 4: at least five hand stencils, an unknown elongate object in negative stencil, patches of red pigment, and a singular fish spine stencil. Local oral tradition from Selpele elders associates the site with turtle hunting, turtle blood and magic were said to produce the art, and the ovoid designs may represent turtle shells. | Alternative_Name: WAI-31

COMMENTS: Description: Brambaem (PEF-3), meaning 'hand stencil' in the Beser Biak language, is located on the southeast edge of a small bay formed by Pef Island. All paintings are red pigment hand stencils, possibly produced by blowing pigment around the hand, located in two alcoves. Panel 1 is approximately 10 m up the cliff face and contains two hand stencils (one right, one left hand) with faded areas of pigment above them. Panel 2 is approximately 3 m up the cliff and contains a single right handprint.

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-53 Mon Ake, meaning 'secret place' in the Wauyai dialect of Ma'ya, is located in the Sabama (red mangrove) area of Kabui Bay, several metres above present mean sea level. The site comprises a single red anthropomorph and a geometric motif to the top left. The anthropomorph has two protrusions from the head, one hand with three fingers raised, and another hand without visible fingers pointing downward. The two protrusions may represent bird plumes or kain (cloth in Papuan Malay), both significant exchange valuables used as headdresses in the past.

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-74 Mol II, meaning 'behind the mountain' in the Laganyan dialect of Ma'ya, is located in northern Mayalibit Bay adjacent to Arway village, on the south side of a steep karst peninsula. The site displays both red and white rock images on a single rock face. Elders at Arway recount that their ancestors lived atop the mountain before monotheist religions, during the hongi raids - Tidore fleet raids to Raja Ampat for slaves and tribute, outlawed by the Dutch in the late nineteenth century. Panel 1 (red): one anthropomorph, a right handprint, and a faded geometric design below, elders at Anday identify the figure as a Ma'ya person adorned with kain on head and waist and holding a shield and knife. The images are located only about 0.5 m above high tide, suggesting relatively recent production. Panel 2 (white): immediately to the right of the red images, depicts a human in a boat and other now-faded designs, unknown to the Arway elders.

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-54 Mlelen Popo, meaning 'manta ray above' and referring to a place where a cross can be seen in the Wauyai dialect of Ma'ya, is located on the eastern face of a large peninsula of Waigeo Island on the western edge of Kabui Bay. Two panels of white pigment art with trace evidence of a brown pigment background are located along approximately 10 m of rock face, close to the modern high tide level. A shell placed in a crevice near the art may be contemporary with the paintings or later. Panel 1, near sea level: crosses, triangles, marine animals (including what appears to be a crab), and anthropomorphs or lizards with slightly bent arms with three fingers. Panel 2: a sailboat image approximately 5 m above present mean sea level, accessible by climbing (unlike the red pigment sites at Lentagin, Mon Ake, and Brambaem which lack accessible handholds).

COMMENTS: Description: WAI-55 Fafag is located on the northeast side of Fafag Island, with one panel of white paintings on a brown pigment background approximately 1 m above the low tide mark, a few centimetres above the high tide mark. The panel is grouped into three clusters. Cluster 1 (left): an anthropomorph or hybrid human-animal motif with uplifted arms and an abstract motif above. Cluster 2 (middle): an anthropomorph or hybrid with raised arms and a cross above, an anthropomorph with uplifted arms, an arrow through its torso, and a cross above, a sailboat with a smaller anthropomorph and a cross below, an anthropomorph with uplifted arms next to a cross enclosed in a circle above another anthropomorph above a forked cross, a curved abstract motif above a trapezoid, a canoe, and a half-circle divided into three segments (the trapezoid and canoe may represent a sailboat, or the trapezoid may depict an island or mountain), geometric motifs (two crosses, a triangle), a face in portrait view, and an anthropomorph with faded or back-positioned arms, below these, a canoe, a small anthropomorph, and abstract motifs resembling the letters E and T. Cluster 3 (right): several small crosses and abstract motifs, an anthropomorph with raised arms, and a curved animal design. Many figures have upraised arms with three fingers and head protrusions possibly representing hair or headdresses. Interlocutor Frans Waiganyam described the scene as a fight between local Ma'ya people and incomers represented by the figure with an arrow through its torso, possibly recalling an undocumented attack on incoming sailors. The scene may date to the late eighteenth or early nineteenth century context of increased Malay, Chinese, and European trade and Malukan raiding, or may reflect an earlier conflict between Ma'ya and Beser Biak or Malukan clans.
